p: Meredith Sloane agreed in writing to the DNA test and fought the rest, and Judge Esquibel signed the order. The scrapings are going to the state lab.
The property record showed Gene cancelled that test himself in November 2007, and on the phone he owned it. He figured the bar fight explained whatever was there.
Dani finally told Ana about the tissue on her father's neck.
Her count showed the red jacket can't pick her father out of twenty one men on his crew, and doesn't put any of the others at the curb either.

Then she remembered that Teo drank Sprite at ten, and called their father Papi when he was scared. She wrote his name under the question, and asked him to drive her to the test. He said yeah in four seconds.
Ana Brennan. Her copy of the 2010 opinion lives in her top drawer.
Luis Ruiz. At Sterling, still Wednesdays at seven.
Teo Ruiz. He's driving Dani to the test.

Tuesday, June 1. The writing part of the test opened that morning, eleven days ahead of the rest of it, and Dani knew because it had been on the kitchen calendar since December in pencil with a box drawn around it. LSAT Argumentative Writing. Fifty minutes at home on her own laptop, with a camera watching her the whole time. No score. The law schools would read it anyway.
Since that yeah, her brother had sent her exactly one more text, the Thursday after: what time. She'd told him. He'd sent back a thumbs up, which from Teo was close to a paragraph.

On the 6:52 she did one question a stop and missed two of eleven, both the same kind, and typed them into the log on her phone, like every miss since October. The log was long now. She scrolled to the top of it once, to the first week, and then put the phone away.

Ana's Tuesday was short. Nothing on the desk but a kitchen timer, a stack of index cards and one last practice passage, about eraser marks on old midterms, and how a changed answer goes from wrong to right about twice as often as the other way, that she'd made Dani read cold at the door. No case, she said. Not tonight. A week from Thursday, the opinion. The twelfth, not a word of it. Tonight's the test. Sit.

June on Federal. The laundromat has a box fan in the door and a man asleep in a plastic chair next to it, and Dicta's asleep on my rug with her feet going. Pencil. Tonight is about the morning itself, because people lose points there that they'd already earned.

Here's the test. Four sections, thirty five minutes each. Two are scored Logical Reasoning, one is scored Reading Comprehension, and one is an extra section that doesn't count, which can be either kind and can sit anywhere in the order. Nobody will tell you which one it is, and how hard a section felt won't tell you either. So as far as you're concerned every section counts, first through last. There are no logic games anymore. They went away in August 2024, and what took their place is more of what you've done all year. This is the test through June 2027, the one you'll sit. Starting August 2027, LSAC changes it: Reading Comprehension first, the unscored questions tucked inside each section, and two breaks, so if your test is later than June 2027, check lsac.org before you go.

After section two you get ten minutes. The test is still running. Your phone stays in the locker, you don't talk to a soul about a single question, you don't touch your scratch paper, and you're back in your chair before the clock runs out. Section three won't start early because you came back early, so use the time. Water, the bathroom, a walk down the hall.

Every question is worth the same, and a wrong answer costs you nothing a blank wouldn't. Read that twice. A blank is the only answer that's sure to be wrong. When one question is eating your clock, it's worth exactly what the easy one three down is worth, so give it its share of the time, put in your best guess, flag it, and go get the easy one. Come back if there's time. With a minute left and three you haven't opened, pick a letter and fill all three, then spend whatever seconds are left reading one of them.

How the exam asks it. You can get to the test center up to thirty minutes early with a valid government photo ID and your LawHub username and password, memorized or on paper, since your phone goes in a locker. LSAC's test day checklist and its dos and don'ts page spell it all out. Read them the week of your test.

One kind of question shows up on nearly every test and asks you to explain something that looks impossible. Two facts, both true, that seem to fight. A ski hill had its snowiest winter in ten years and sold fewer lift tickets than the winter before. The stem asks what most helps resolve the discrepancy, or explain it.

Don't pick a side. The question already told you both facts are true, so an answer that says one of them is wrong is wrong. You want the fact that makes both of them sensible at once. Say the highway over the pass was closed by snow on half the weekends that winter. Now the snow and the empty lifts fit together. The same snow did both.

The traps explain one fact and leave the other exactly as strange as it was. Lift tickets cost more this year? That's a reason for fewer tickets, and it says nothing about the snow. What you want goes through both facts, and usually it's a difference nobody mentioned: a different group of people, a different stretch of time, something counted two different ways.

How the exam asks it. Stems ask which answer most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy, explain the paradox, or reconcile the findings. Check your choice against both facts. If it only touches one, it isn't the answer.
Everything else you'll see Saturday you already know. Here it is in one place, so you hear it all together once.

Must be true is the strictest question on the test. The answer has to follow from what's given, every time, with nothing added. Most strongly supported is a step looser: the passage has to back the answer better than any other, even if it doesn't guarantee it. On both, the trap is the answer that goes one word too far. Some becomes most. Can becomes will. The right answer usually sounds smaller than you want it to.

A necessary assumption is something an argument can't do without. Negate the choice, and if the argument falls apart, you've got it. A flaw question asks you to say what went wrong in plain words before you look at the choices, and the usual ones haven't changed since December. A trait that fits many people treated as if it fits one. A sample that picked itself. A cause read into two things that happen together. A requirement treated as a guarantee.

And the blank at the end of an argument, the one that says so and then leaves you a line. Fill it with what the premises support. Not the most exciting thing they could support. Read it back with therefore in front of it, the way we did in October, and listen to whether it holds.

How the exam asks it. Stems for these say must be true, most strongly supported, the argument depends on assuming, most vulnerable to criticism, and most logically completes the argument. Saturday you won't have time to name every flaw. You'll have time to ask what the argument needed and didn't have.

A court opinion is a passage with a job to do. Somebody appealed. The court says what they argued and what it decided, then why, one issue at a time. The main point is nearly always the decision itself, affirmed or reversed. Don't confuse one reason the court gives along the way with the point. One issue isn't the opinion.

Purpose asks why the author wrote a passage or a paragraph. Main idea asks what it says. Function asks what one piece is doing for the whole: giving a reason, answering an objection, setting up a contrast, closing the matter. Organization asks how it's built, so watch the order, and who chose it. Courts often take issues in the order the lawyer raised them. That's the lawyer's order, and it tells you nothing about what the court thought mattered most.

Meaning in context is the one people miss, because they already know the word. The question isn't what the word means in a dictionary. It's what it means in that sentence. Standing can mean upright, or rank, or a person's right to bring a case at all, and only the sentence around it can tell you which. When a question asks what the court would agree with, stay inside what the court said. A court that calls evidence sufficient has said a jury could find something. It hasn't said the jury had to.

How the exam asks it. Stems ask for the main point, the primary purpose of the passage or a paragraph, what a phrase most nearly means as it's used, the function of a sentence, how the passage is organized, and what the author would most likely agree with.

The writing part opens eight days before the test window, and you do it at home. You can do it after the test too, but nobody sees your score until it's done, so do it first. Fifty minutes. Fifteen are for reading and planning, and you can move on after five, which I wouldn't do. Thirty five are for writing. You get an issue people really do disagree about and three or four perspectives on it, a few sentences each. You take a position and answer some of the others.

Answering them is the job. Anybody can say what they think. The essay worth reading takes the strongest thing the other side said, says it fairly, and then says why it doesn't settle the question, or how much of it you'd keep. If your essay could have been written without reading the perspectives, you didn't do the task.

It isn't scored, and it still counts. Your score won't be released until an approved sample is on file, and the schools read it. No paper, no pencil. You type your notes into a box on the screen, with a camera on you and nothing on the table but your ID, tissues, foam earplugs and a clear bottle of water with the label peeled off.

One note on the video below. It was made before the test moved into test centers, so skip its tip about remote proctors. And LSAC sends schools every score you have on file, not just your highest one.

How the exam asks it. LSAC calls it LSAT Argumentative Writing. You can start it eight days before the test window opens, at home, on your own laptop or desktop with a webcam. Do it early. Processing can take a few weeks, and nobody sees your score until it's through.
What a sentence is doing, worked.

Role questions come up a couple of times on most tests, and they're quick points if you've found the conclusion first. The stem quotes one claim from the argument and asks what part it plays. The choices are descriptions: it's the main conclusion, it's a premise offered in support, it's an intermediate conclusion that supports the main one, it's a view the argument opposes, it's background, it's a concession the arguer makes before turning.

Here's the order. Find the main conclusion. Then find the claim in the stem and ask three things in a row. Is it the conclusion? Does anything support it? Does it support anything? A claim that supports the conclusion and has nothing under it is a premise. A claim with support under it and the conclusion over it is an intermediate conclusion. A claim the arguer doesn't believe, introduced with some people say or critics argue, is the opposing view. A claim the arguer grants and then argues past, introduced with admittedly or it's true that, is a concession.

Work one. A city planner says this. Some residents argue that the new bike lanes have made Fourth Street more dangerous, since two cyclists were hurt there in the spring. But injuries on Fourth fell by a third in the year after the lanes went in, so the lanes have made the street safer, not less safe. They should stay. The stem quotes the lanes have made the street safer and asks its role. The main conclusion is that the lanes should stay. The fall in injuries supports the claim about safety, and the claim about safety supports keeping the lanes. Support under it, the conclusion over it: that's an intermediate conclusion. A choice that calls it the main conclusion is the usual trap, because it sounds like the point. Ask what it's for. It's there to hold up the lanes should stay.

Now ask about the two cyclists. That's evidence offered for a view the planner rejects. The right description says something like it's offered in support of a position the argument opposes. The trap says it's a premise the planner relies on. The planner mentions it, and doesn't rely on it.

Two things people miss. A claim can be true and still be the view the argument opposes, since the cyclists really were hurt. The question is about the job, not the truth. And the same claim can play different roles in different arguments. If the planner had said the injuries prove the lanes are dangerous, and then given up the lanes, the cyclists would be premises. Read the role off this argument, not off what the sentence usually means.

How the exam asks it. Role stems ask which one most accurately describes the role played in the argument by a quoted claim. Find the main conclusion first, then ask whether the claim is supported, supports something, or is the opposing view.
Main point and attitude, in a passage.

Two of the most common reading questions ask what the whole passage is for and how the author feels about it. Main point and attitude. They feel easy and cost people more points than anything else in a set, because the wrong answers are true sentences from the passage.

For the main point, find what the author is willing to stand behind at the end. Not the most interesting fact. Not the first paragraph's view, which is often the one the author takes apart. The main point is the claim every paragraph serves. Test a choice by asking whether the first paragraph is there to set it up and the last paragraph is there to finish it. A choice that only covers the middle paragraph is too narrow. A choice that claims more than the last paragraph is too broad.

For attitude, find the words that carry judgment. Elegant. Unconvincing. Admittedly. Too quickly. Most authors on this test hold a moderate view and state it plainly, so the right answer usually pairs a judgment with a limit: qualified approval, measured skepticism, respectful disagreement. When a choice has one strong word, like dismissive or enthusiastic, go find the line that earns it.

And keep one more line apart. The question may ask about the author's attitude toward one thing in the passage, a theory, a study or a group of critics, and not toward the subject. An author can like a field of research and doubt one study in it. Read the stem for what the attitude is toward, and then read only the lines about that.

How the exam asks it. Main point stems ask which most accurately expresses the main point or central idea of the passage. Attitude stems ask for the author's attitude toward something, and an author can be critical of one study and warm toward the field it came from. Check the first and last paragraphs for the main point, and the judgment words for attitude.

Here's how I'd spend the writing time. The first fifteen minutes are for thinking, and the screen gives you a box for notes. Use all fifteen. Read the issue and every perspective once. Then write four lines in the box. Your position, in one sentence, with its limit: what you'd do, and how far. The strongest perspective against you, in your own words. What you'd grant it. And why it still doesn't change your answer, or how it changes the plan.

Then a rough order for the essay. An opening that states the position, not the debate. A paragraph for your best reason, with an example. A paragraph that takes the strongest objection seriously and answers it. A paragraph that handles a second perspective, more briefly. And an ending that says what you'd do and stops. That's four or five paragraphs in thirty five minutes, which is plenty if the thinking is already done.

While you write, keep two rules. Use the perspectives as evidence, not decoration. Quoting one and moving on doesn't count as engaging it. And keep your claims the size of your reasons. If you've given one good reason, say should, not must. The readers at a law school are looking for exactly what this book has been teaching: a conclusion, the support under it, and an honest look at what would weaken it.

Leave three minutes at the end to read it once. Fix the sentence that says the opposite of what you meant. Don't start rewriting paragraphs. It isn't scored, and the schools that read it would rather see a finished, plain essay than a half fixed fancy one.

How the exam asks it. LSAT Argumentative Writing gives fifteen minutes for prewriting analysis and thirty five for the essay. Take a position, engage the strongest perspective against it, and size your claims to your reasons.

Ana set the kitchen timer to thirty five minutes and laid it face down on the desk. On the twelfth you're going to hit one that won't let go of you, she said. Section two, probably. That's where the nerves wear off and the pride comes in. You'll read it three times. You'll be sure you're one more read from it.

She wrote on a card in capitals and turned it around. EVERY QUESTION COUNTS THE SAME. A WRONG ANSWER COSTS NOTHING A BLANK WOULDN'T. THE ONE IN FRONT OF YOU IS WORTH WHAT THE EASY ONE THREE DOWN IS WORTH. SO.
Finish it, Ana said. Out loud.
A. "So it gets its fair share of the clock and not a second more. Then I flag it and go get the easy one."
B. "So I do the hard ones first, while I'm fresh, and I let the easy ones carry the end of every section."
C. "So the hard ones are probably in the section that doesn't count, and I can let them all go without a fight."
D. "So I skip every hard one the second I see it, and I don't look at any of them until the very end."
Ana turns the timer back over without starting it. Its share, she says. Say that to yourself in there. A question doesn't get more of your clock for being rude to you.

That's the one. Pencil down. Complete the argument. Every question is worth the same, and the minutes are shared among them. What those premises support is a rule about time: a hard question gets a fair share and no more, and you move on and come back. Nothing on the card says skip on sight, and nothing says hard ones don't count.

Wednesday, June 2, at half past five, she wrote it at the kitchen table. She'd cleared the table to the wood. The laptop, her license, a water bottle with the label peeled off, and a dish towel taped over the window in the back door, because the rules said no glass. The camera made her show it the whole room, slowly, all the way around: the stove, the calendar, the basement door shut, and the hook by the back door where her mother's lanyard still hung, the hospital badge turned to the wall. Then fifteen minutes to read and plan, and thirty five to write, and for the first time since October no pencil in her hand.

At seven her father called. What'd they have you write about? I can't tell you, Pa. I agreed not to. I clicked a box. Good, he said. Don't. He sounded pleased, a man who'd lived by a rule card since 2008. The next Wednesday he asked who was driving her Saturday, and she told him, and he asked her to say it again. Then: He drives careful. He always did. And: What do you two talk about, all that way in a truck? Nothing, Pa. Same as always. Okay, he said, and she couldn't tell what kind of okay it was. Neither of them said a word about the board. It was her move, and had been since his queen went home, and he didn't ask for it.

Thursday, June 10, Ana opened her top drawer and took out the copy Dani had seen once, in November. Stapled, gone soft, pencil down every margin, a coffee ring on the back. She laid it open on the desk to the first page and then to the last.

Colorado Court of Appeals, opinion announced Thursday, June 17, 2010, page one. Defendant, Luis Ruiz, appeals the judgment of conviction entered on a jury verdict finding him guilty of second degree murder. He raises nine contentions. He argues that the trial court erred in instructing the jury, in declining to excuse a juror who may have fallen asleep during testimony, in admitting the victim's telephone statement to his sister as an excited utterance, and in five other rulings, and that the evidence was insufficient to identify him as the person who struck the victim. We address the first eight in the order he presents them. We affirm.

The same opinion, page eleven. Section nine. Remaining contentions. Defendant's remaining contentions require little discussion. Taken in the light most favorable to the People, the evidence that defendant wore a red work jacket that night, that he had fought with the victim inside the bar less than an hour before, and that the victim's blood was on his cuff was sufficient for the jury to find that he was the man the witness saw strike the victim. The judgment is affirmed.
Last passage, Ana said. You've read yours. Read mine once like it's a stranger's. Seventeen years next Thursday. She didn't look at it. Main point. One sentence.
A. The evidence proved he was the man who struck the victim outside the bar that night.
B. The trial court got a few of its rulings wrong, but none was bad enough to change the result.
C. The court turned down all nine of his contentions and let the conviction stand.
D. The evidence was enough for a jury to find he was the man the witness saw strike the victim.
Affirmed, Ana says. Nine in, nine out. That's the point, she says, and it's the first word anybody reads on the thing and the only one anybody remembers. She takes her hand off the page.

Right. Now say why. Main idea. Page one sets out nine contentions and says the court affirms, and page eleven disposes of the last of them and affirms. The point that covers the whole opinion is that none of the nine succeeded and the conviction stands.

Ana turned through the pages in between one at a time, slowly, wetting her thumb on the corners like a bank teller. The jury instruction took two and a half pages. The juror took two, the call to Shannon took two more, and the five issues after that got shorter and shorter, down to a paragraph or so apiece. Then page eleven, one paragraph at the top and nothing under it but white paper.
A. It starts with his strongest argument and works its way down to the weakest, which gets the end.
B. It names nine, takes eight one at a time in the order he raised them, then ends the last in a paragraph.
C. It argues every issue from both sides, his and the State's, and then rules on all nine at the end.
D. It tells the story of the night first, then the trial, and after that it turns to his arguments.

In the order he presents them, Ana reads off page one, and taps it with the pencil. He didn't present anything, she says. I did. That's my order, all eleven pages of it, and they walked it exactly the way I laid it out in the fall of 2009.

Good. That's how you read it. Organization. Page one names nine contentions and says the court will take the first eight in the order presented. Page eleven handles what remains in one paragraph and affirms. That's the structure.
Ana laid the eraser end of her pencil on the desk just under page eleven, below the two words at the top of it, careful not to touch the paper. Remaining contentions.
Meaning in context, she said. Not what it means. What it means there.
A. Whatever he'd argued that the court hadn't already taken up in the first ten pages.
B. His strongest arguments, the ones a court saves for the end because they matter most.
C. The questions still open after the trial, the ones the jury never got the chance to decide.
D. The arguments he was still making on appeal, after he'd let go of some of the others.
Left over, Ana says. Like the coffee in the pot at the end of the day. Then she says, to the page and not to Dani, that it's a polite word, and courts keep a lot of those around.

That's the one. Pencil down. Meaning in context. Page one says the court will take up the first eight contentions, and page eleven begins with the remaining ones. Set there, remaining means the ones left over after the first eight.

Before she left that night Ana gave her two things. The copy, still open to page eleven, which as far as Dani knew had never once left the drawer. Bring it back when you're done with it. And a stapled report, eight pages. Practice set for tomorrow night. Three more questions on the opinion, I wrote them down for you. Then this. Then bed. She'd sent the report to a pathologist in Denver the week before. Before she calls me and tells me what she thinks it says, I want you to have read it yourself.

Friday, June 11, Joel sent her home at three. He stood in his doorway with his reading glasses pushed up on his head while she shut her computer down. Monday you can tell me about it, he said. Not the questions. How it felt. In September you'll need it for the essay.

That night she had the opinion on the kitchen table with the lamp pulled close. Ana's card was clipped to the front, three questions in capitals. WHAT'S THE ONE SENTENCE DOING? WHY WRITE THE LAST PARAGRAPH AT ALL? WHAT WOULD THEY AGREE WITH?
Beside the sentence, in pencil gone gray, somebody had written a small 1 and put a circle around it. She knew whose pencil. She didn't know what year.

She read the sentence again, slower. The evidence that he wore a red work jacket that night, that he'd fought the victim inside the bar less than an hour before, and that the victim's blood was on his cuff was sufficient for the jury to find that he was the man the witness saw strike the victim. The first question, then.
A. It lists three pieces of the evidence against him that the jury heard at the trial.
B. It gives the court's only reason for rejecting his claim that the evidence didn't identify him.
C. It admits that the identification was the weakest part of the case, and then it decides it anyway.
D. It sets out the rule the court used to decide all nine of his contentions together at once.

The only reason, and it's three facts in one sentence with and between them. She runs a pencil she doesn't need under it. Jacket, fight, blood. The court never says how many men wore that jacket. The sentence works without anybody saying it, and that's the trouble with the sentence.

Right. Now say why. Function of a detail. The sentence takes the identification challenge, the last of the nine, and answers it: the jacket, the fight and the blood were enough for a jury. It's the court's reason for rejecting that claim.
WHY WRITE THE LAST PARAGRAPH AT ALL? Ana had put a pencil line under AT ALL.
It was a fair question. The court had spent ten pages on eight arguments. It could have stopped at the bottom of page ten, and it wrote one more paragraph instead.
What's the primary purpose of page eleven?
A. To explain why the trial evidence was enough for a jury to find he was the man in the red jacket.
B. To show other courts that the identification issue was the most serious one in the whole appeal.
C. To scold his lawyer, gently, for burying a court under nine arguments when one would have done.
D. To answer whatever was left of the appeal, so the ruling covered every argument before it said affirmed.
That's the job a last paragraph does in an opinion like this. You can't affirm with an argument still sitting there unanswered. So it got answered, in a sentence, because a sentence was all it took.

Good. That's how you read it. Primary purpose. The paragraph disposes of the one contention the opinion hadn't yet reached, identification, and then states the result. It's there to finish the appeal, so the affirmance covers everything he raised.
WHAT WOULD THEY AGREE WITH? The last question on the card. She held page eleven under the lamp and read the sentence slowly, the way she'd read her own testimony on the bus in October.
Sufficient. Of all the words they could have used, they'd used that one.
Which statement is the court committed to by what it wrote on page eleven?
A. The jacket was the most important piece of evidence the jury had for finding that he was the man.
B. No one else who was at the bar that night had on a red work jacket like the one he wore.
C. The witness had a clear enough look at the man's face to be certain that it was him at the curb.
D. A jury may rely on several facts taken together to find that the defendant struck the victim.
Three things joined by and, and a jury allowed to add them up. That much they'd sign. How many men the first of the three fit, the sentence never says, and it reads just fine without saying it.

That's the one. Pencil down. Would agree. The court held that the jacket, the fight and the blood together were sufficient for the jury to find identity. It's committed to the idea that a jury may combine several facts to reach that finding.

Then the report. She'd had every page of the case in her hands by now except this one. There was a copy in Phil's second banker's box too, and she'd lifted it out and set it aside twice, the way you step around a soft place in a floor.

Report of autopsy, Travis Hensley, October 28, 2007, from the findings and the opinion. Laceration, two and a half centimeters, above the left eyebrow. Superficial. Does not reach the bone. Bruising of the left brow and upper eyelid. Depressed fracture of the back of the skull, with bleeding over and into the brain. Fingernail scrapings and clippings collected from both hands, released to Detective G. Vigil. Opinion. Cause of death: blunt force injury of the head. The fatal injury is the depressed fracture at the back of the skull. The laceration above the left eyebrow is a separate, superficial injury and is non-contributory. Manner of death: homicide.

She read it the way Ana said to, like a passage. Main point, the fracture killed him. Detail, two and a half centimeters. Meaning in context, non-contributory: it was there, and it had nothing to do with how it ended. She wrote the answers in the margin in pencil and they were right, and she sat there with them anyway.
Thirty one years old. Six foot two, page one said. A sheet metal worker, a Rockies fan having a bad night. She'd known his name since she was fifteen and had never once read where he was hurt.

At a quarter to eleven she had LawHub open on the laptop, and the full practice test she'd been saving, and the log on her phone. This week she'd missed more than any week since March. She typed it into the log. Worst week since March. Not ready. One more full test tonight and I'll know where I stand in the morning.
She read it back like it was somebody else's.
Her plan in the log depends on which assumption?
A. That a full test she starts at eleven tonight would tell her how she'll do at eight tomorrow.
B. Nothing she can find. She starts the full test at eleven, and when it's done she starts another.
C. That this week's misses came from not knowing the material, and not from a week of bad sleep.
D. That she'd have missed fewer this week if Ana had handed her more practice tests to work on.

Deny it and the plan falls over. If a test at eleven can't tell her about eight, it isn't worth the sleep. She shuts the laptop. She sets two alarms and puts the phone across the room, and lies there until one, which beats four.

Right. Now say why. Necessary assumption. The plan says one more test tonight will tell her where she stands tomorrow. That depends on tonight's tired score predicting tomorrow's rested one. Negate it, and the reason for the test is gone.
Saturday, June 12. She'd slept some, and she was up before the alarm. She was making coffee she didn't need when the phone buzzed on the counter.
A text from Prometric. Reminder: your appointment is Saturday, June 12, at 8:00 AM, Greenwood Village. Please arrive 30 minutes early with a valid government issued photo ID.

At 6:25 the truck was at the curb, twenty minutes early. He'd washed it. She could see where the water had dried in streaks on the hood. Two coffees in the cup holders, one with her name on the lid in Bianca's writing, a burrito in foil on the dash, and under the burrito a folded sheet with a purple horse on it holding a pencil. GOOD LUK TIA.

He said morning. She said morning. Then 270, and 25 south with the sun already up and low over the plains on their left, the radio low on a station that was mostly ads, and her brother not saying one thing, his hands at ten and two.
Five weeks he hadn't answered the text about Pa. Then yeah. in four seconds, and now this. She looked at the lid with her name on it and tried to get both facts to sit in the same truck.
A. Work had him on doubles at the bus garage for five weeks, and this week it finally let up on him.
B. He feels bad about the party and the pawn text, and this is how he's trying to make it up to her.
C. Pa's the thing he can't talk about. A ride he can say yes to, and drive without saying a word.
D. Bianca made him say yes and wash the truck, the way she makes him go to Lupe's school things.
So she doesn't bring up Pa. She doesn't bring up anything. You washed the truck. It was dirty. Past the Broadway exit he reaches over and turns the radio down one more notch.

Good. That's how you read it. Resolve the paradox. The two facts are a long silence after a text about their father and a fast yes to a ride. If what he can't do is talk about Luis, and the ride asks nothing of him but driving, both facts fit at once.

The test center was in an office building in the Tech Center, beige carpet and a water cooler and a row of chairs, and she was the third one there. She left the prep book on the truck seat. Inside it would only have gone in a locker. The envelope was in it, marking her page. She knew it was. She thought about taking it out, and didn't.

A man behind a counter looked at her license and then at her, a second each. Phone off, into a gray locker with Lupe's horse, the burrito and her water. Her username and password she said to herself once more, as she had on the bus all week. They gave her a station by the wall with a computer on it, gray earmuffs the size of a pilot's, two pencils and a short stack of scratch paper, and there was a camera up in the corner of the ceiling. She read the statement on the screen and agreed to it. Then section one came up, with its clock running in the corner.

Section two had a question in it about a ferry schedule that she read three times and couldn't make give. She flagged it and went on. With four minutes left she came back, read it once more, saw it, and changed her answer. Eraser marks, she thought, and moved on.

Then the break. Ten minutes on a timer. She told the proctor, waited for the nod, and walked out to the lockers for her water, past the phone she couldn't touch. A young guy at the next locker was shaking his hands out. That last section, he said to her. Brutal. That's got to be the experimental, right? I can't talk about it, she said. He looked at her like she'd said it in Latin, then like he remembered, and went off toward the bathroom.
Section two had been the worst of it, by a lot. Standing at the cooler, she caught herself thinking the thing she'd told Ana she wouldn't think.
That one was the hardest. So that's the one that doesn't count. So I'm fine.
Her reasoning at the cooler is most vulnerable to which criticism?
A. It assumes section two went badly, when she flagged only one question and got back to it in time.
B. Nothing's wrong with it. If everybody in the room found section two hard, they're all in one boat.
C. It reads which section doesn't count off how hard one felt, and the test never tells anybody that.
D. It forgets a wrong answer costs nothing, so a hard section can't hurt her score at all.

Hard is a feeling she had at a water cooler. Which section doesn't count is a fact nobody in that building knows. So section two counted, as far as she's concerned, and three would, and four. She finishes the water, sits back down with two minutes to spare, and waits with her hands in her lap for the timer to run out.

That's the one. Pencil down. Flaw. Her reasoning uses difficulty as evidence that section two was the unscored one. The extra section could be the easiest of the morning or the worst, and nothing on the screen marks it, so how it felt tells her nothing about whether it counts.

Section three was Reading Comprehension, and it went like the last eight months said it would. Section four didn't. Twenty three questions in, the clock in the corner was down to its last minute, and there were three she hadn't opened.
Every question worth the same. Nothing off for a wrong one. One minute.
What do those facts most strongly support about the three she hasn't opened?
A. One of the three is probably easy enough that she could still work it out inside a minute.
B. She should pick whichever letter she's used the least this section, since it's due.
C. Guessing on all three will raise her score on this section by at least one question.
D. Filling in all three can only tie a blank or beat it, never do worse.

She clicks the same letter on all three. Then she opens the last one and reads the stem, because there are forty seconds, and forty seconds is a stem. She changes nothing. The section ends before she's sure it has.

Right. Now say why. Most strongly supported. With no deduction for wrong answers and every question worth the same, a guess can only tie a blank or beat it. That's all the facts support. They don't promise a gain.

It was twenty past twelve and ninety degrees on the asphalt when she came out, and she had no idea how she'd done. She knew she couldn't say a word about it to anybody. The phone came back to life in her hand with one text, from that morning.
A text from Ana. Pencil down when they tell you. Then go eat.

The truck was in the far corner of the lot under the one tree, with the engine running for the air. Teo had the prep book on the dash. The envelope wasn't in it. It was in his hand, back side up. WHO WAS THE KID? in her capitals, and under it his name.

She'd left it there. She'd known it was in the book when she shut the truck door on it, and she'd let it ride on the seat beside him all morning. He'd found it early, she could tell. He'd sat out here under the tree with it the whole time, so it wouldn't be in that room with her.

He didn't ask how it went. He held the envelope out so she'd see he'd seen it, and then didn't let go of it. You put my name on it, he said. Not angry. Tired, like a man who'd sat four hours with it, which he had. I was there, Dani.
She got in and shut the door, and the cold air hit her. In Pa's truck, he said. When he drove out of that lot, I was in it.
Pa had said it to Gene in 2007, and to her on a hundred Wednesdays, and across a cardboard board in April. Went home. By myself.
A. "Then you know where Pa went after he left. You were right there with him."
B. "Then Pa didn't drive home by himself. That part isn't true."
C. "So you were there when that man got hit at the curb. You saw Pa."
D. "Then Pa's lied to me about that whole night, Teo. Every word he ever said."

Teo says that part, yes. He says it to the envelope. Two rows over a woman in hospital scrubs gets out of an old Corolla, and a girl comes out of the building with her license still in her hand, and the woman hugs her right there between the cars, and Dani watches them instead of her brother.

Good. That's how you read it. Must be true. Since 2007 Luis has said he drove home by himself, and now Teo puts himself in that truck when it pulled out. If Teo's right about that, then by himself can't be. Nothing else has to follow from what he said.

She was so tired her hands felt like they belonged to somebody in the back seat. Four hours of being careful with every word on a screen, and now this, in a parked truck that smelled like Bianca's coffee.

He still had the envelope. He turned it over to the front. He'd read it already, she could tell by how he didn't hurry. He read it again anyway, MAYBE HE DID IT across the top in her capitals and every line under it, slowly, like a parts manual. Then he set it on the dash with his own name up.

He asked her if she thought it was Pa. He asked it quietly, to the envelope and not to her, because that was what it said across the top in her own capitals. She'd been carrying it around in the back of her book since December.

She didn't answer him. All morning she'd picked whichever answer had to be true, five choices at a time, a hundred times or near it, and nobody had ever handed her a sheet with a line on it for this one.

Out past the tree a man in a polo shirt was walking a girl with a clear plastic bag to a minivan, his arm around her shoulders, and somebody honked twice at somebody in the next row, happy about something. Her vent was on high, aimed at her knees. She left it.
He said it to the windshield. I hit him. The man. Dani, I'm the one that hit him.
